title: Eastern Carolina Vinegar Sauce
subtitle: Thin, sharp BBQ dressing for pulled pork
excerpt: Eastern Carolina vinegar sauce is a thin, sharp dressing made from cider vinegar, chilli flakes, black pepper, and a little salt. It's applied to pulled pork while the meat is still hot, soaking in rather than sitting on top. No tomato, no sweetener beyond a pinch.
sourceNotes: Eastern North Carolina vinegar sauce is the oldest style of American barbecue dressing, pre-dating tomato-based sauces. This is the standard household recipe documented across North Carolina barbecue writing.

recipe.yieldDescription: about 200 ml, enough for one pulled pork batch
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and keep in a sealed jar in the fridge for up to a month.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps for a month in the fridge. The flavour mellows slightly over time.

content.text: Eastern Carolina vinegar sauce is not a coating: it's a dressing that soaks into pulled pork while the meat is still hot, lightening the richness and adding a sharp, peppery bite. The recipe takes five minutes and needs no heat. What makes it work is the balance: sharp vinegar, warmth from chilli and pepper, and salt to carry both.
Combine {{cider-vinegar}}, {{chilli-flakes}}, {{black-pepper}}, and {{sea-salt-flakes}} in a jar or small jug. Add {{dark-brown-sugar}} if using. Stir until the salt and sugar dissolve.

Let the sauce stand for at least ten minutes before using. This allows the chilli flakes to bloom slightly and the flavours to integrate. Taste: it should be sharp, lightly spiced, and just barely sweet. Adjust the seasoning.
Pour over freshly pulled pork while the meat is still hot, so the sauce soaks in rather than pooling on the surface. Use about half at the mixing stage and serve the rest alongside.

items.symptom: The sauce tastes too harsh and acidic
items.cause: Cider vinegar can vary in sharpness between brands.
items.fix: Add a little more sugar or a pinch more salt to round it. The sauce should be sharp but not unpleasantly so.

items.symptom: The sauce has no real heat
items.cause: Chilli flakes lose potency over time.
items.fix: Taste your chilli flakes before using: if they're pale and dusty rather than red and oily, replace them. Add an extra half-teaspoon if you want more heat.

items.cause: Sugar needs a little agitation to dissolve in cold vinegar.
items.fix: Stir vigorously for 30 seconds, or warm the vinegar very gently in a small pan before mixing.

items.symptom: The sauce is too thin and runs off the meat
items.cause: It's meant to be thin: that's the style.
items.fix: Pour it over the pork while the meat is still in the bowl before plating, so it soaks in. If you want a thicker sauce, use the Kansas City BBQ sauce recipe instead.

content.text: This vinegar sauce is the oldest style of American barbecue dressing, used in the Carolinas long before tomato-based sauces took over. In Eastern North Carolina it is still the standard for whole-hog barbecue. Adding tomato to the sauce is considered heresy. Keep a jar in the fridge: it works on fried chicken and grilled sausages too.
